title: How Long, O LORD? A Prayer From the Sickbed
summary: David, weak in body and shaken in soul, begs the LORD not to discipline him in anger but to heal and deliver him. He describes nights soaked in tears and eyes worn out by grief. Then, abruptly, his tone changes: the LORD has heard his weeping, and his enemies will be put to shame.
story: Psalms 3 to 5 were prayers against human enemies. Psalm 6 turns inward to a suffering that is physical and spiritual at once: bones in agony, a soul deeply distressed, and the fear that God himself is against him. The enemies are still present (verses 7, 8, and 10), but the deeper trouble is God's apparent anger. This is the first psalm in the collection to ask “How long?”, a cry that will return again and again (Psalm 13 is built around it). The Psalter is teaching its readers that the life of God's people includes seasons when prayer feels unanswered, and that such seasons can be spoken aloud to God.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David and gives musical directions but no occasion. Nothing in the text ties it to a known event in his life, and the language of illness, tears, and enemies is general enough to fit many situations. Some interpreters suppose a serious illness that opponents took as a sign of God's judgment; others read the bodily language as the way the Hebrew poets described deep distress of any kind.

From early in Christian history the church grouped Psalm 6 with Psalms 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143 as the seven Penitential Psalms, prayed especially in times of repentance and during Lent. Readers should notice, though, that Psalm 6 contains no explicit confession of sin. It asks God not to rebuke in anger, which suggests the psalmist fears his suffering is discipline, but the psalm's focus is on mercy and rescue rather than on naming a particular wrong.
cultural:
The heading's “Sheminith” comes from the Hebrew word for eighth. It may refer to an eight-stringed instrument, to a lower octave, or to a particular tune; no one knows for certain. It appears again in the heading of Psalm 12 and in 1 Chronicles 15:21, where Levite musicians lead the music with lyres “according to Sheminith”.

Many in the ancient world, including many in Israel, assumed a close link between sickness and sin, and a sick person could find that friends and enemies read his illness as God's verdict against him (the book of Job argues against drawing that conclusion too quickly). Verse 5 reflects an Old Testament picture of death. Sheol is the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a shadowy place below the earth where the dead go, cut off from the praise and worship of the living community. The psalmist's argument is simple: if I die, one voice that praises you goes silent. The fuller hope of bodily resurrection comes into view only later in the Old Testament (Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2) and is revealed in Christ.
literary: Psalm 6 is an individual lament, and it shows the classic shape of the form. It opens with an address and plea (verses 1 to 3), gives reasons why God should act (verses 4 and 5), describes the suffering in detail (verses 6 and 7), and then turns suddenly to confidence that the prayer has been heard (verses 8 to 10). That sudden turn, found in many laments, has puzzled readers. Some think a priest spoke a word of assurance in worship between verses 7 and 8; others think the change happened in the psalmist's own heart as he prayed. The poem uses heavy repetition: the name LORD appears eight times in ten verses, and the broken cry “How long, O LORD, how long?” in verse 3 breaks off mid-sentence. Verse 10 echoes the start: the words for distress (verse 3) and turning (verse 4) return, now applied to the enemies.

outline.t: Heading and plea: do not rebuke me in anger, heal me
Turn and save me, for the dead cannot praise you
Nights of weeping, eyes worn out with grief
The LORD has heard: the enemies turn back

doctrines.note: The psalm gives the sufferer permission to describe pain in plain detail, to ask “how long”, and to say that God seems angry. Lament is part of faith, not a failure of it.

Though it names no specific sin, the psalm asks for mercy rather than claiming innocence, and the church has long used it as a prayer of repentance. It appeals not to the psalmist's worth but to God's covenant love (verse 4).
The turn in verses 8 to 10 shows that prayer can move from anguish to assurance, not because the circumstances have changed yet, but because the one praying knows he has been heard.

words.note: Yasar, to discipline. The word covers instruction, correction, and chastening, often the way a father trains a son (Deuteronomy 8:5). The psalmist does not deny that God may discipline him; he asks that it not be done in wrath. Discipline in the Bible belongs to relationship, which is why the psalmist can appeal to God's love in the same breath.

Sheol, the realm of the dead. The Old Testament pictures it as a place below, where all the dead go, marked by silence and separation from the worshiping community. It is not the same as the later idea of hell as a place of punishment, though older English versions sometimes translated it that way. In verse 5 it is the place where praise stops.

Chesed, loving devotion or steadfast love. In verse 4 it is the reason God should save: “because of Your loving devotion”. The psalmist cannot appeal to his own strength or record, so he appeals to God's covenant faithfulness, which does not depend on the worthiness of the one who asks.

christ: Two New Testament moments echo this psalm. In John 12:27, facing the cross, Jesus says that his soul is troubled, words that closely match the Greek translation of verse 3, and the Gospel writers show him praying with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7). The Son of God entered the kind of anguish this psalm describes. And in Matthew 7:23 and Luke 13:27, Jesus uses the words of verse 8, telling evildoers to depart from him. The sufferer's word to his enemies becomes the judge's word at the last day. These are echoes and patterns rather than predictions. The psalm's fear that death silences praise is also answered in the New Testament's announcement that Christ has broken death's hold by rising from the dead.

hard.q: Does verse 5 mean the psalmist didn't believe in life after death?
hard.a: Verse 5 says that no one praises God in Sheol, and similar lines appear elsewhere (Psalm 30:9; Psalm 88:10-12; Isaiah 38:18). Many scholars conclude that much of the Old Testament had only a dim view of life beyond death, with fuller hope emerging later in texts like Daniel 12:2. Others point to passages such as Psalm 16:10-11 and Psalm 49:15 as signs of earlier hope, and note that verse 5 is an argument in prayer, not a doctrinal statement about the afterlife: its point is that the worshiping community on earth loses a voice when one of its members dies. Both readings agree that the Old Testament does not present death as natural or good, and that the full answer comes with the resurrection of Jesus.

questions: The psalmist cries “How long?” without apologizing for it. What keeps you from bringing that kind of honest complaint to God?
Verse 6 describes tears that soak a bed at night. How can a church make room for people in that kind of grief without rushing them?
The psalm turns from anguish to confidence before anything outward has changed. Have you ever known that kind of turn, and what brought it?
